content: 1. The Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) focuses on addressing viral hepatitis, including hepatitis C virus (HCV), as a significant public health issue. It incorporates evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis, treatment, and care. 2. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a major cause of chronic liver disease, leading to approximately 399,000 deaths annually. In 2019, an estimated 58 million people were living with chronic HCV infection, with a disproportionately high burden in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). 3. HCV antibodies, also referred to as anti-HCV antibodies, are detectable in the blood within two to three months of HCV infection or exposure. These antibodies indicate prior or ongoing exposure to the virus. 4. HCV RNA refers to the viral genome of HCV, which can be detected and quantified in serum using nucleic acid testing (NAT). This is a critical marker for diagnosing active infection. 5. HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) is a nucleocapsid peptide (p22) released into plasma during viral assembly. It can be detected early in the course of infection and throughout its progression. 6. Chronic HCV infection is characterized by the persistent presence of HCV RNA or HCVcAg in serum, along with positive serology for HCV antibodies. 7. Viraemic infection refers to the active presence of HCV in the bloodstream, as measured by HCV RNA. This is often referred to as an active or ongoing infection. 8. Cirrhosis is an advanced stage of liver disease marked by extensive hepatic fibrosis, nodularity, architectural disruption, and impaired hepatic circulation. 9. Decompensated cirrhosis is a stage of liver disease where clinical or laboratory signs of cirrhosis are evident. Clinical features include portal hypertension (ascites, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy), coagulopathy, or liver insufficiency (jaundice). Other features may include hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, pruritus, fatigue, arthralgia, palmar erythema, and edema. 10. Laboratory findings in cirrhosis and portal hypertension often include low serum albumin, low platelet count, and prolonged prothrombin time. 11. Sustained virological response (SVR) is defined as undetectable HCV RNA in the blood at a specific time point after completing treatment, typically at 12 or 24 weeks (SVR12 or SVR24). Achieving SVR is considered a cure for HCV. 12. HCV non-response occurs when HCV RNA remains detectable in the blood throughout the treatment period. 13. HCV relapse refers to the reappearance of detectable HCV RNA after initially achieving undetectable levels during or at the end of treatment. 14. HCV viral breakthrough is defined as the reappearance of detectable HCV RNA during ongoing treatment after initially achieving undetectable levels. 15. Serological assays are diagnostic tests that detect the presence of antigens or antibodies, typically in serum or plasma, but also in capillary/venous whole blood or oral fluid. These include rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and laboratory-based immunoassays such as enzyme immunoassays (EIAs), chemiluminescence immunoassays (CLIAs), and electro-chemiluminescence immunoassays (ECLs). 16. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are immunoassays that detect antibodies, antigens, or nucleic acids and provide results in less than one hour. Most RDTs can be performed using capillary whole blood collected via finger-stick sampling. 17. Enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) are laboratory-based serological immunoassays that detect antibodies, antigens, or both. They require plasma or serum collected through venepuncture. 18. Nucleic acid testing (NAT) is a molecular technology, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription-mediated amplification (TMA), that detects small quantities of viral nucleic acids (RNA, DNA, or total nucleic acid) either qualitatively or quantitatively. 19. Point-of-care (POC) testing is conducted at the site of clinical care, with results provided to the patient or caregiver on the same day to enable timely clinical decision-making. 20. Reflex viral load testing involves automatically performing an HCV RNA (or HCV antigen) test for individuals with an initial positive HCV antibody screening result. This can be implemented through laboratory-based or clinic-based reflex testing. 21. Laboratory-based reflex testing uses a single clinical encounter and one blood draw for an initial HCV antibody test. If positive, the same or a duplicate specimen is used for immediate reflex HCV RNA or antigen testing, with results provided for both tests. 22. Clinic-based reflex testing involves a single clinical visit for an initial rapid diagnostic HCV antibody test using a capillary blood sample. If positive, a second blood sample is collected immediately for HCV RNA testing, either sent to a laboratory or tested on-site using a POC assay. 23. Clinical/diagnostic sensitivity of a test refers to its ability to correctly identify individuals with the infection or disease (true positives). 24. Clinical/diagnostic specificity of a test refers to its ability to correctly identify individuals without the infection or disease (true negatives). 25. Positive predictive value (PPV) is the probability that a positive test result accurately indicates the presence of the infection or disease. 26. Negative predictive value (NPV) is the probability that a negative test result accurately indicates the absence of the infection or disease. 27. Analytical sensitivity or limit of detection (LoD) is the lowest concentration of a measurement that can be consistently detected in 95% of specimens under routine laboratory conditions. 28. Age groups are defined for treatment recommendations: adults (≥20 years), adolescents (12–19 years), older children (6–11 years), and younger children (3–5 years). 29. Key populations at increased risk for HCV, HBV, and HIV include men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, people in prisons, sex workers, and transgender individuals. These groups often face legal and social barriers to accessing prevention and treatment services. 30. Vulnerable populations, such as migrants, refugees, and indigenous populations, are particularly susceptible to HBV/HCV infection due to specific contexts or situations. They may also face barriers to accessing care. 31. Community-based testing includes outreach approaches such as mobile testing, home-based testing, workplace testing, and testing in schools or other venues. 32. Facility-based testing occurs in healthcare settings, including primary care clinics, hospitals, and specialized clinics for HIV, viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and tuberculosis (TB). 33. Decentralization involves delegating authority and resources to lower levels of the health system, such as regional or community levels. 34. Differentiated service delivery simplifies and adapts viral hepatitis services to meet the needs of individuals and optimize health system resources. 35. Integration refers to the co-location and sharing of services across different disease areas, such as providing HCV testing and treatment alongside HIV, TB, STI, or antenatal care services. 36. Task-sharing redistributes tasks from higher-level healthcare providers to trained lay providers, including community members. 37. Linkage to care involves actions that support individuals testing for HBV/HCV to engage with prevention, treatment, and care services appropriate to their status. 38. Person-centered care focuses on organizing healthcare around the needs and expectations of individuals and communities rather than diseases. 39. The WHO aims to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. However, significant gaps remain in HCV testing and treatment, with only 21% of individuals diagnosed and 13% treated as of 2019. 40. Achieving HCV elimination requires simplifying care pathways to improve access to testing and treatment. Updated WHO guidelines emphasize direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment for children aged ≥3 years, simplified service delivery, and the use of POC HCV RNA assays and reflex testing.
